newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-BHP sets sights on global gas market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BHP sets sights on global gas market.

text.p: Australian resources and energy group, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), said on Tuesday it aimed to expand its global natural gas business, just over a week after the sudden departure of its petroleum chief.

BHP chief executive John Prescott said BHP's future success was likely to be more closely tied to the global gas market than oil. "We are not saying we would rather be a gas company than an oil company. What we are saying is that over a period of time we think the world is going to switch more to gas as an energy," Prescott told reporters after a speaking at a business luncheon.
Prescott said BHP believed the world was moving towards natural gas as an alternative to nuclear energy and the company wanted to take advantage of this opportunity.
The comments reinforced the oil unit's core nature after the resignation of its head, John O'Connor, earlier this month.
O'Connor, previously a BHP director, was said to have argued for the hiving-off of petroleum from the rest of BHP, a proposal that had been considered and rejected by the board.
BHP's main gas interest is its one sixth stake in the North West Shelf project in Western Australia which supplies liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Japan and gas to the domestic market.
"The indications are that our gas reserves are building faster than our oil reserves. I expect that our gas reserves will be far more broadly-based than the North-West Shelf," Prescott said.
Asked if BHP was looking at becoming involved in gas pipeline network in Asia, Prescott said: "Yes we are interested in the development of appropriate pipelines."

In his luncheon address Prescott reaffirmed BHP's committment to sell non-strategic or underperforming assets by May 1998. He added the company was on track to reduce its debt by A$4 billion in the same period.

Listing the group's underperforming assets, Prescott named the steel assets at Whyalla, in South Australia, New Zealand, Newcastle in New South Wales and two Asian roll-forming businesses, which he said BHP intended to sell.

"All other businesses in steel - and there are 40 of them -- are earning above eight percent return on capital," Prescott said, adding that about 20 steel operations achieved better than 15 percent return.
BHP had largely rebuilt its Australian steel facilities and was looking to cut capital employed in this area. "In short we don't need a lot of capital in the steel group," Prescott said.

BHP suffered management turmoil earlier this month which apart from petroleum chief O'Connor's departure also saw the resignation of minerals division chief Dick Carter and iron ore head Geoff Wedlock.
Carter and Wedlock's resignations coincided with cost overruns at BHP's Pilbara hot briquetted iron (HBI) project in Western Australia.
Prescott said the company was working hard to manage risks and hold management accountable for results.
"In filling the vacancies we have today, we are going first to clearly delineate the roles of these positions to take into account the changes and needs I have talked about," he said.
Prescott said the company was currently looking for three new board members including a replacement for O'Connor but said the next two or three appointments would be non-executive positions.
BHP shares closed 2.2 cents higher at A$17.13.
